title: Command-Line Programs
summary: Writing C tools that behave well in a terminal - reading options from argv by hand, flags with values, the conventions of -h, -- and combined short flags, getopt where it exists, standard input, output and error, exit codes with EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE, reading lines of any length, and working in pipelines.

cards.q: Why should error messages go to `stderr`?
cards.a:
So redirected output holds only the real results

`prog > out.txt` captures `stdout` only. Messages on `stderr` still reach the person on the terminal and do not mix with the data.

cards.q: What does `--` on a command line mean?
cards.a:
The end of the options

Everything after `--` is an argument even if it starts with `-`, so `-notes.txt` is taken as a file name.

cards.q: A tool finished but one of its three input files was missing. What exit code fits the conventions?
cards.a:
A non-zero code such as 1

Any failure should give a non-zero code, after printing the problem to stderr, so scripts can notice it.
